arc_intro:
FQ-171 — Ravi Krishnan (Head of Engineering)

Let's go deeper on actually managing a running instance, not just launching one and walking away. Two things: I want a look at how order-service's instances get their initial configuration when they boot, and I want Session Manager properly set up on everything, not just theorized about.

Also, heads up — karthik-dev mentioned he's not 100% sure where his laptop with the SSH keys is right now. Probably nothing. But let's make sure we're not one lost laptop away from a real problem.

— Ravi
arc_outro:
Ravi Krishnan — FQ-171 update:

Good timing on the Session Manager setup — turned out karthik-dev's laptop really was gone, and with it, the only copy of the private key for one of the instances. A month ago that would've meant rebuilding it from scratch. Instead, you got in through Session Manager without missing a beat, generated a fresh key pair, and kept working. That's exactly why we set it up properly instead of just talking about it.

Next: let's talk about what happens when someone makes a change directly on a running instance and there's no record of it anywhere — and what a proper AMI/snapshot strategy actually looks like instead.

— Ravi

tasks.scenario: Ravi wants a look at how order-service's EC2 instances get their initial configuration when they first boot up, as part of tightening how the team manages running instances day to day.
tasks.question: Which two AWS-native mechanisms are most relevant to check first for how an instance configures itself and learns about its own environment at boot time?
options: A) CloudFront and Route 53 — these control how traffic reaches the instance, which is unrelated to self-configuration

B) User data (a script that runs at first boot to bootstrap the instance) and the instance metadata service (which lets the instance query its own details like instance ID, IAM role credentials, and more, from within itself)
C) Security groups and NACLs — these are the only things that affect what an instance can do at boot
D) The AMI's name tag — this is the only source of configuration information available to a running instance
tasks.explanation: User data and the instance metadata service are exactly the two things that matter here — user data bootstraps the instance at first boot, and the metadata service lets a running instance ask AWS about itself (instance ID, IAM role creds, etc.) without needing anything hardcoded. Security groups control network access, not configuration — different concern entirely.

tasks.ren_wrong: A bit think again — security groups network access control does, configuration not. User data and metadata service correct answer.

tasks.question: An EC2 instance's user data script installs some packages and writes a config file on first launch. If the instance is later STOPPED and then STARTED again (not terminated/relaunched), does the user data script run again automatically?
options: A) Yes — user data always re-runs on every single boot, including after a stop/start cycle

B) By default, no — user data runs only once, at the instance's very first boot after launch. A stop/start cycle does not re-trigger it unless the instance is specifically configured to re-run user data on every boot
C) User data never runs at all unless manually triggered by an administrator
D) User data only runs if the instance type is changed during the stop

what_to_find: The database password and a live payment API key are hardcoded directly in plaintext in the user data script

User data is visible to anyone who can query the instance's metadata service from within the instance (169.254.169.254/latest/user-data) — this is not a hidden or encrypted location, it's readable by design
This means any process, script, or person with shell access on the instance can trivially read out the production DB password and live payment API key, just by querying the metadata endpoint
This is a much bigger exposure than a typical config file, since user data persists as long as the instance exists and is queryable at any time, not just at boot
tasks.correct_fix: Remove the hardcoded secrets from user data entirely. Store DB_PASSWORD and RAZORPAY_API_KEY in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (as SecureString) or Secrets Manager instead, and have the user data script (or the application itself, at startup) fetch them securely via an IAM role at boot time — never embed real secrets directly in user data.

tasks.scenario: A week after fixing notification-worker's IAM role and confirming Session Manager works across the fleet, karthik-dev calls in a panic — his laptop, with the only copy of the .pem private key for one of the order-service instances, was stolen. He assumes the instance now needs to be terminated and completely rebuilt from scratch.
tasks.error_shown:
$ ssh -i lost-key.pem ec2-user@<instance-ip>
Permission denied (publickey).

(the .pem file no longer exists anywhere — it was only ever saved on the stolen laptop)
tasks.diagnosis: SSH access genuinely depends entirely on possessing the private key file — with it gone, SSH into this instance really is impossible, and karthik-dev's instinct that SSH access is lost is correct. But Session Manager access does NOT depend on the key pair at all — it authenticates purely through IAM. Since this instance already has the IAM role and SSM Agent properly configured (from the earlier fleet-wide fix), it remains fully reachable through Session Manager, completely independent of the lost key.
tasks.fix: Connect to the instance via Session Manager (no key needed at all). From inside that session, generate a new SSH key pair, add the new public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and securely distribute the new private key to karthik-dev going forward — restoring SSH access without ever needing to terminate or rebuild anything.
tasks.explanation: This exact real payoff of setting up Session Manager properly earlier — SSH key completely lost-a even if, IAM-based access different vazhi giving. This in C4.2a theoretical-a we saw 'why Session Manager is better' concept, ippo REAL in crisis real-a use but moment.

tasks.scenario: While reviewing metadata service usage across the fleet, ananya-analyst asks a security-adjacent question: 'I read that the metadata service has caused real breaches at other companies through something called SSRF. Should we be worried?'
tasks.question: What's the accurate, current answer regarding metadata service security?
options: A) There's no real risk — the metadata service has never been involved in any real-world security incident

B) It's a real, documented risk pattern — older instances/AMIs may still default to IMDSv1, where a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in an application could trick it into fetching IAM credentials from the metadata endpoint on the attacker's behalf. IMDSv2 (token-based, session-oriented) closes most of this gap and should be the default/required setting on all instances
C) The only fix is to disable the metadata service entirely on every instance, which has no downsides
D) SSRF only affects on-premises servers, never cloud instances like EC2
